specPoints.text: understand that an RNA molecule is single stranded and contains uracil (U) instead of thymine (T)

primer.text: DNA stores the plan; RNA carries the working copies. This note fixes the two headline differences — single-stranded, uracil instead of thymine — then names the three working types, mRNA, tRNA and rRNA, whose roles return in the protein synthesis note straight after this one.

lessons.title: One Strand, One Swapped Base
lessons.opening: RNA is the working copy of the genetic message: a single polynucleotide strand, built on ribose sugars and phosphates, carrying A, G and C like DNA but replacing thymine with uracil, and appearing in the cell as mRNA, tRNA and rRNA.
keyPoints: RNA stands for ribonucleic acid and is a polynucleotide.
Its bases are adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil.
Uracil takes the place that thymine holds in DNA.
RNA is single-stranded, one polynucleotide chain.
mRNA, tRNA and rRNA are the taught RNA types, with mRNA the transcript copy of a gene.

low.restatement: RNA is one strand long and swaps thymine for uracil.
low.analogy: A photocopy of one page, written in slightly different ink colours.
low.examPointer: The two headline differences are single-stranded and uracil.

medium.restatement: The chain of ribose-phosphate units carries projecting bases, and the base inventory U-without-T identifies RNA instantly.
medium.analogy: A ladder with only one rail, its rungs painted in a recognisably different set of colours.
medium.examPointer: Attach a role to each RNA type when asked to name them.

check.stem: Which base does RNA carry in place of thymine?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Thymine is the DNA base that uracil replaces.
Both molecules carry adenine.
Both molecules carry guanine.

check.stem: How many strands does an RNA molecule have?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Two coiled strands describe DNA.
No triple-stranded nucleic acid is taught.
A molecule with bases still has a strand.

options.text: A long chain of many linked nucleotides
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Proteins are polypeptides.
Sugars are components, not the whole chain.
Lipids are unrelated to nucleotides.

check.stem: Which RNA type is the transcript copy of a gene?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
tRNA carries amino acids during translation.
rRNA forms part of the ribosome.
DNA is the original, not the transcript.

check.stem: Which sugar forms part of each RNA nucleotide?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
That sugar belongs to DNA.
Glucose is a respiratory substrate.
Lactose is a milk sugar, unrelated here.

check.stem: State the two headline differences between RNA and DNA.
check.modelAnswer: RNA is single-stranded and contains uracil instead of thymine.

check.stem: List the three RNA types named in the note.
check.modelAnswer: Messenger RNA, transfer RNA and ribosomal RNA.

check.stem: Explain why uracil's presence makes RNA recognisably different from DNA.
check.modelAnswer: Every base inventory that shows U without T identifies a single-stranded RNA chain rather than the thymine-carrying double helix.

check.stem: A diagram shows one uncoiled strand bearing the bases A, U, G and C. What molecule has been drawn, and which DNA base is absent from it?
check.modelAnswer: The diagram shows RNA, and thymine is the DNA base absent from it, replaced by uracil.

glossary.definition: Ribonucleic acid, a single-stranded polynucleotide containing uracil.
A long chain of many linked nucleotides.
The base that takes thymine's place in RNA.
Messenger RNA, the transcript copy of a gene.
